result.question: State of the art (as of July 2026) in AI coding-agent governance and harness design — the problem space of the claude.md-workflow repo: project instruction files (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md-style), lifecycle hooks, deterministic verification gates, persistent agent memory/working-state across sessions and compaction, behavioral guardrails against scope creep/overclaiming/sycophancy, git-level enforcement, task contracts, and parallel multi-agent orchestration (worktree isolation, orchestrator/reduce patterns, adversarial review). Survey and compare best practices from: Anthropic (Claude Code, Agent SDK, skills/hooks/subagents), OpenAI (Codex, AGENTS.md), Google (Gemini CLI/Jules/Antigravity), Microsoft (GitHub Copilot agents, AutoGen/agent frameworks), NVIDIA (agent toolkits/NeMo), xAI (Grok agents/coding); and non-Western labs: Moonshot AI (Kimi K2.5 agentic training), Zhipu/Z.ai (GLM-5.x coding agents), DeepSeek (agentic/tool-use practices), Tencent (recent Hunyuan model launch and agent tooling), MiniMax (M-series agentic models), Alibaba Qwen if relevant; plus respected independents: Nous Research (Hermes 4/Hermes agent), Fundamental Research Labs (Peter Wang co-founder), the team behind the Ornith-1.0 LLM, tinygrad/George Hotz's approach to minimal harnesses, and any other influential open agent-harness projects (e.g. OpenHands, SWE-agent, Aider, Cline, Devin/Cognition). For each: what they prescribe for instruction-file structure and length, memory persistence, verification/eval gating, multi-agent patterns, and prompt-vs-deterministic enforcement. Identify convergent consensus, notable divergences (especially Western vs Chinese lab practices), and concrete, citable insights that should shape a 2026 rewrite of a drop-in governance kit for coding agents. Note if any named entity cannot be verified to exist (e.g. 'Ornith-1.0') rather than guessing.
result.summary: As of July 2026, coding-agent governance has converged on a clear architecture across Anthropic, OpenAI, and GitHub/Microsoft: short, hierarchical, nearest-file-wins instruction files (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, the latter now a Linux Foundation-stewarded cross-vendor standard used by 60k+ projects); an explicit split between advisory prompt-level instructions and deterministic harness-level enforcement (lifecycle hooks, permission gates, Stop-hook verification gates); runnable pass/fail checks as the primary quality mechanism with an escalation ladder from in-prompt iteration to hard gates; and git-worktree isolation as the standard concurrency-safety mechanism for parallel multi-agent work. Adversarial-review research (Refute-or-Promote, arXiv 2604.19049) supplies the strongest citable warning: 80+ agents unanimously endorsed a non-existent OpenSSL vulnerability that only an empirical test killed, so consensus and LLM review must be subordinate to deterministic empirical validation, ideally with a cross-model critic to break correlated blind spots. The one verified non-Western data point (Zhipu's GLM-5) shows a divergent bet on model-side asynchronous agent RL rather than harness-side scaffolding. For a 2026 governance-kit rewrite, the actionable prescriptions are: aggressively prune instruction files (Anthropic's removal test; OpenAI's 32 KiB hard cap), split guidance into nested per-directory files, move every must-happen rule from prose into hooks/permission gates, gate task completion on executable checks rather than agent self-report or reviewer consensus, and isolate parallel agents in worktrees with fresh-context, diff-only adversarial reviewers whose findings are treated as noisy signals, not mandates.

findings.claim: Convergent consensus: instruction files must be short, and vendors now enforce or prescribe brevity. Anthropic officially instructs users to aggressively prune CLAUDE.md — the test for each line is 'would removing this cause mistakes?' — warning that bloated files cause the model to ignore instructions. OpenAI enforces the same principle deterministically: Codex caps combined AGENTS.md content at 32 KiB by default (project_doc_max_bytes) and silently stops loading files beyond it, with docs recommending splitting instructions across nested directories rather than growing one file.
findings.evidence: Anthropic (verbatim): 'Keep it concise. For each line, ask: "Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?" If not, cut it. Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions!' OpenAI (verbatim): 'Codex stops adding files once the combined size reaches the limit' (32 KiB default); silent truncation corroborated by openai/codex issue #7138. Both are live primary vendor docs fetched 2026-07-14.

findings.claim: Convergent consensus: hierarchical, nearest-file-wins instruction resolution is the standard structure. Codex resolves instructions via global scope (~/.codex, AGENTS.override.md then AGENTS.md) followed by a walk from Git root to cwd, at most one file per directory, nested files overriding ancestors. The AGENTS.md spec prescribes the same for monorepos — nested per-package files with nearest-file precedence — citing OpenAI's main repo containing 88 AGENTS.md files as a real-world example.
findings.evidence: Codex docs verbatim: 'Files closer to your current directory override earlier guidance' and 'Codex includes at most one file per directory.' agents.md verbatim: 'Agents automatically read the nearest file in the directory tree, so the closest one takes precedence' and 'at time of writing the main OpenAI repo has 88 AGENTS.md files.'

findings.claim: AGENTS.md has become the de facto cross-vendor instruction-file standard with formalized neutral governance: it emerged from OpenAI Codex, Amp, Google's Jules, Cursor, and Factory, is used by over 60,000 open-source projects (verifier's independent GitHub search found ~158k matching files, so the figure is conservative), and is now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation (announced Dec 2025 alongside Anthropic's MCP donation). Codex treats it as the primary governance mechanism, automatically reading AGENTS.md files before doing any work — though loading is mandatory while compliance remains prompt-level and advisory.
findings.evidence: agents.md verbatim: 'used by over 60k open-source projects'; 'now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation.' Codex docs verbatim: 'Codex reads AGENTS.md files before doing any work.' Verifier independently ran GitHub code search (total_count=157,952, incomplete_results=false) and cross-checked LF press release of 2025-12-09. Note: the mandatory-read claim carried a 2-1 vote; open Codex issues (#6502, #6666, #4466) document inconsistent application despite reading.

findings.claim: Convergent consensus on prompt-vs-deterministic enforcement: every major Western vendor draws an explicit line between advisory prompt instructions and deterministic harness enforcement, and prescribes moving must-happen rules to the harness. Anthropic states CLAUDE.md is advisory while hooks are deterministic ('use hooks for actions that must happen every time'); a Stop hook can block turn completion until a check passes (overridden after 8 consecutive blocks). The Agent SDK exposes lifecycle hooks (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, SessionStart, SessionEnd, UserPromptSubmit) as callbacks that validate, log, block, or transform behavior, plus a deterministic permissions system (allowed_tools pre-approval, e.g. a read-only agent limited to Read/Glob/Grep). GitHub's cloud agent defaults to permission-gating every write action, with autonomous 'autopilot' as explicit opt-in after trust is established.
findings.evidence: Anthropic verbatim: 'Unlike CLAUDE.md instructions which are advisory, hooks are deterministic and guarantee the action happens.' GitHub verbatim: 'By default, the cloud agent asks permission before each write action. Switch to autopilot once you have established trust.' SDK docs confirm hook names and permissions semantics verbatim. Caveat: allowed_tools is a pre-approval allowlist, not a hard restriction — it is inert under bypassPermissions mode.

findings.claim: Convergent consensus on verification gating: the top prescription across vendors is a runnable pass/fail check as the arbiter of completion, with an escalation ladder of strictness. Anthropic's lead best practice is giving the agent a verifiable check (tests, build exit code, linter, screenshot diff) and choosing how hard it gates: in-prompt iteration → /goal conditions re-checked every turn → deterministic Stop hooks → second-opinion verification subagents. The AGENTS.md spec ties instruction files to the same expectation: agents execute programmatic checks listed in the file and fix failures before finishing. GitHub's Agent Merge extends gating to the git level: the agent drives CI back to green, addresses review feedback, and merges only when user-specified conditions are met.
findings.evidence: Anthropic verbatim: 'As a deterministic gate: a Stop hook runs your check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes.' agents.md FAQ verbatim: 'The agent will attempt to execute relevant programmatic checks and fix failures before finishing the task.' GitHub verbatim: 'drive CI back to green, address feedback, or merge when your conditions are met.' Caveats: AGENTS.md check-running is prescribed expectation, not mechanical enforcement; Agent Merge rides GitHub's existing merge conditions rather than adding a new enforcement primitive, and the Copilot app is in technical preview.

findings.claim: Convergent consensus on multi-agent orchestration: git-worktree isolation is the industry-standard concurrency-safety mechanism, and orchestrator/subagent patterns are first-class. Anthropic recommends worktree-isolated parallel sessions, agent teams with a team lead, and Writer/Reviewer session pairs; its Agent SDK supports subagents with specialized instructions and restricted tool lists, invoked via an Agent tool, with parent_tool_use_id attribution per subagent execution. GitHub's Copilot desktop app independently converged on the same design: every parallel agent session runs in its own git worktree, managed automatically.
findings.evidence: Anthropic verbatim: 'Worktrees: run separate CLI sessions in isolated git checkouts so edits don't collide.' GitHub verbatim: 'Every session runs in its own git worktree, a real, isolated copy of your branch.' SDK docs confirm AgentDefinition (prompt + tools restriction) and parent_tool_use_id verbatim. GitHub app reached GA across Copilot tiers 2026-07-07; cloud sessions use hosted isolated environments instead of local worktrees.

findings.claim: Adversarial review works but has sharply documented limits, yielding three citable design rules. (1) Reviewer over-reporting: Anthropic warns that a reviewer prompted to find gaps will report some even when the work is sound, and chasing every finding causes over-engineering; its prescribed mitigation is a fresh-context subagent that sees only the diff and criteria. (2) Consensus is not correctness: in the Refute-or-Promote study, 80+ agents including ten dedicated adversarial reviewers unanimously endorsed a non-existent Bleichenbacher padding oracle in OpenSSL's CMS module; only a single empirical test killed it — motivating a mandatory deterministic empirical-validation gate rather than prompt-level consensus as final arbiter. (3) Cross-model critique breaks correlated blind spots: a critic from a different model family found correctness errors in 3 of 19 (~16%) fixes that same-family review had approved, plus 3 additional missed bugs, in the libfuse campaign.
findings.evidence: Anthropic verbatim: 'A reviewer running in a fresh subagent context sees only the diff and the criteria you give it... Chasing every finding leads to over-engineering.' Paper verbatim: 'ten dedicated reviewers unanimously endorsed a non-existent Bleichenbacher padding oracle in OpenSSL's CMS module; it was killed only by a single empirical test' and 'CMC found correctness errors in 3/19 (~16%) same-family-approved proposed fixes.' Confidence capped at medium because arXiv 2604.19049 is a single-author, non-peer-reviewed preprint with small n and no replication (the cross-model claim drew only medium verifier confidence), and the same paper's headline ~79%-kill-rate claim was refuted in verification. The Anthropic over-reporting warning alone is high-confidence.

findings.claim: Memory persistence is converging on layered mechanisms: instruction-file memory plus resumable session state, with cross-surface memory as the 2026 frontier. Anthropic treats CLAUDE.md/.claude/CLAUDE.md as the project memory/instruction mechanism, loaded via filesystem configuration (.claude/ and ~/.claude/, restrictable via settingSources); its SDK persists session state as local JSONL, resumable by session ID or forkable to explore alternatives (versus an Anthropic-hosted event log for Managed Agents). GitHub ships persistent cross-session, cross-surface agent memory ('Memory++' and '/chronicle') spanning desktop app, CLI, VS Code, and github.com as of mid-2026.
findings.evidence: SDK docs verbatim: 'Resume sessions later, or fork them to explore different approaches' and 'Session state | JSONL on your filesystem | Anthropic-hosted event log.' GitHub verbatim: 'Memory++ and /chronicle give Copilot continuity across devices and over time. Query context from sessions started in the app, CLI, VS Code, or on GitHub.' Caveat: Memory++//chronicle have little third-party documentation and ship in technical preview; underlying Copilot Memory was repo-scoped with 28-day expiry in its Jan-Mar 2026 public preview.

findings.claim: Verified Western-vs-Chinese divergence (limited to one data point): Zhipu AI positions GLM-5 as a paradigm shift 'from vibe coding to agentic engineering' — autonomous end-to-end software engineering — and invests in model-side capability via a new asynchronous RL infrastructure that decouples generation from training plus novel asynchronous agent-RL algorithms for long-horizon interactions. This contrasts with the Western pattern of harness-side governance (hooks, gates, permissions); Zhipu ships GLM coding models to run inside third-party harnesses (including Claude Code-compatible plans) rather than building its own enforcement layer.
findings.evidence: GLM-5 technical report abstract (GLM-5 Team, Zhipu AI/Tsinghua, Feb 2026) verbatim: 'designed to transition the paradigm of vibe coding to agentic engineering' and 'we implement a new asynchronous reinforcement learning infrastructure that drastically improves post-training efficiency by decoupling generation from training.' The model-vs-harness contrast is a hedged inference consistent with Zhipu's shipping posture, not a stated claim; training gains are self-reported. This is the only Chinese-lab claim that survived verification — Moonshot, DeepSeek, Tencent, MiniMax, and Qwen practices remain unverified, so the divergence generalization rests on n=1.

result.caveats: Coverage is uneven: verified claims exist only for Anthropic, OpenAI/AGENTS.md, GitHub/Microsoft (Copilot), one independent arXiv methodology paper, and Zhipu AI. Nothing survived 3-vote verification for Google (Gemini CLI/Jules/Antigravity), Microsoft AutoGen, NVIDIA NeMo/agent toolkits, xAI, Moonshot AI, DeepSeek, Tencent Hunyuan, MiniMax, Alibaba Qwen, Nous Research, Fundamental Research Labs, tinygrad/George Hotz, or the open harnesses (OpenHands, SWE-agent, Aider, Cline, Devin) — so the 'convergent consensus' findings reflect the verified subset, not the full requested survey, and the Western-vs-Chinese divergence rests on a single lab (Zhipu). The 'Ornith-1.0 LLM' named in the question could not be verified to exist and no claims about it were produced; it should be treated as unverifiable rather than real. arXiv 2604.19049 (Refute-or-Promote) is a single-author, non-peer-reviewed preprint with self-reported case studies; its headline claim (~79% kill rate over a 31-day campaign) was refuted in verification (1-2 vote), so only its OpenSSL false-consensus anecdote and cross-model-critic result should be cited, with the small-n qualifier. Several GitHub features (Copilot app cloud agent, Agent Merge, Memory++//chronicle) are in technical preview, and Memory++//chronicle lack third-party documentation. AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md compliance is prompt-level everywhere: mandatory loading does not mean enforced obedience (documented Codex issues show inconsistent application; the 32 KiB truncation is silent). All vendor-doc claims were verified live on 2026-07-14 against fast-moving documentation; specifics (8-block Stop-hook override, 32 KiB default, hook names) may change within months.
openQuestions: What do Google (Gemini CLI/Jules/Antigravity), the major Chinese labs beyond Zhipu (Moonshot Kimi K2.5, DeepSeek, Tencent Hunyuan, MiniMax, Qwen), and leading open harnesses (OpenHands, SWE-agent, Aider, Cline, Devin) actually prescribe for instruction files, hooks, and verification gating — and does the model-side-RL vs harness-side-scaffolding divergence hold beyond the single verified Zhipu data point?

How well do agents actually comply with instruction-file directives in practice — given documented Codex issues of reading-but-ignoring AGENTS.md and Anthropic's admission that long files get ignored, is there rigorous empirical data on compliance rates versus file length, structure, or placement?

Does the Refute-or-Promote result (unanimous multi-agent consensus on a non-existent vulnerability; cross-model critics catching ~16% bad fixes) replicate at scale in peer-reviewed or industrial settings, and what is the optimal cost/precision trade-off for mandatory empirical-validation gates in a drop-in governance kit?

How will AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md conventions reconcile under the Agentic AI Foundation's stewardship — will a unified resolution/precedence spec emerge (including standardized hook or check-declaration syntax), and should a 2026 governance kit target AGENTS.md as primary with CLAUDE.md as an alias?

refuted.claim: An adversarial, stage-gated multi-agent review pipeline (Refute-or-Promote) killed roughly 79% of ~171 defect candidates before disclosure over a 31-day campaign across 7 targets, with an 83% prospective kill rate on a consolidated-protocol subset (n=30), demonstrating that most LLM-generated defect findings are false positives that structured adversarial gating can filter out.
